title: Topic: Firm Performance and Growth
text:
These are the most commonly used outcome indicators in EU firm-level impact evaluations. Where possible, use administrative data (business registries, tax records) rather than self-reported figures to reduce measurement error.

1.1 Turnover growth

Definition: Change in total annual sales revenue over the evaluation period
Metric: % change in turnover from baseline to endline; log of turnover
Data source: Administrative (tax records, business registry) or primary survey



1.2 Value added

Definition: Value of output minus the value of intermediate inputs; a measure of the firm’s contribution to GDP
Metric: Total value added in € (turnover minus purchases of goods and services); % change over evaluation period
Data source: Administrative (tax records) or primary survey



1.3 Labour productivity

Definition: Output produced per unit of labour input — a core competitiveness indicator
Metric: Value added per employee (€); % change over evaluation period
Data source: Administrative or primary survey (requires both value added and employment data)



1.4 Total factor productivity (TFP)

Definition: Output not explained by inputs — captures how efficiently a firm uses all its resources
Metric: Estimated using production function methods (e.g. Olley-Pakes, Levinsohn-Petrin); requires data on output, capital, labour, and materials
Data source: Administrative (requires linked firm-level panel data)



1.5 Employment growth

Definition: Change in the number of people employed by the firm
Metric: % change in full-time equivalent (FTE) employees from baseline to endline; log of employment
Data source: Administrative (social security records, business registry) or primary survey



1.6 Wage growth

Definition: Change in average wages paid by the firm, reflecting improvements in job quality and productivity
Metric: % change in average gross wage per employee; total wage bill growth
Data source: Administrative (social security or tax records)



1.7 Export performance

Definition: Whether and how much the firm sells in foreign markets
Metric: Export participation (yes/no); share of turnover from exports (%); log of export value
Data source: Administrative (customs data) or primary survey



1.8 Firm survival

Definition: Whether the firm remains in operation over the evaluation period
Metric: Binary indicator (firm active / closed); survival rate across the sample
Data source: Administrative (business registry)

section: How many firms do I need?
text:
How many firms do I need?
Once you know who is eligible, the next question is whether enough firms are available to measure an impact. Three things determine the answer.


Expected impact
The smaller the effect you expect, the more firms you need to detect it.


Desired precision
More certainty about the answer requires more observations.


Budget and capacity
Every firm in the study needs support, monitoring, and surveys.



Pool too small? Loosen the eligibility bar, or widen the ranking bins.

title: How
text:
Public draw or private draw?



Public lottery


A public draw, for example pulling names from a hat.
Advantage: transparent and fair.
Disadvantage: the comparison group may change its behaviour once it knows the result.




Private lottery


A lottery run behind the scenes.
Advantage: avoids the comparison group reacting to a public result.
Disadvantage: less visibly fair.




In practice, many World Bank-supported evaluations run the draw as a secure, documented, computerized procedure that can be re-checked afterwards.

title: How
text:
Why a lottery?


Fair
In SMART Romania, every eligible firm had the same chance of receiving a grant. Selection could not be influenced by connections or favouritism.


Defensible
Rules reduce bias. Across several studies, even expert judges struggle to predict which firms will succeed.


Efficient
One online survey serves as application, eligibility check, and baseline data collection.



Citations For the “defensible” card: Chen et al. (2022) on judicial favouritism in Kenya; Fafchamps and Woodruff (2017), Identifying gazelles, World Bank Economic Review 31(3); McKenzie and Sansone (2019), Predicting entrepreneurial success is hard, JDE 141. title: How
text:
Why randomize?
Now that both groups have been followed over time, the final question is how to attribute any differences to the programme.

“What would have happened without the programme?” Randomization makes it possible to answer this question.




Firms drawn in the lottery


Received digitalization grants.




Firms not drawn


No grants; surveyed identically.



Because the lottery created two comparable groups, the difference between them is the true impact of the programme.

title: How
section: Five practical ways to randomize your programme
text:
Five practical ways to randomize your programme
SMART Romania used one approach: the lottery. Many programmes need a different design.

  
    Lottery
    How: randomly select who gets the programme, by public or private lottery.
    Best when: eligibility is clear and the programme is oversubscribed.
  
  
    Multiple treatment arms
    How: randomly assign different versions of the programme, with or without a control group.
    Best when: you want to know which design works best, not just whether it works.
  
  
    Randomized phase-in
    How: everyone gets the programme eventually, in a random order. Those still waiting are the comparison group.
    Best when: budget or capacity cannot cover everyone at once.
  
  
    Randomized intensities
    How: vary how much of the programme a firm gets, for example 100%, 50%, or 0% of eligible employees.
    Best when: spillovers within or between firms are a concern.
  
  
    Encouragement design
    How: randomize who gets extra outreach to take up the programme, since it cannot be denied to anyone.
    Best when: take-up is voluntary and the programme itself cannot be withheld.
  

SMART Romania✓ Used a lottery (design 1)✓ Oversubscribed programme✓ 1,038 eligible firms

Randomly assign firms to different versions of the programme, plus a comparison group.

title: Topic: Technology Readiness Level
text:
Use at baseline and endline. TRLs are the standard scale used by the European Commission — including in Horizon Europe and ERDF-funded R&D programmes — to assess the maturity of a technology or innovation. Measuring TRL at baseline and endline captures whether the intervention has helped firms advance their technologies along the development path from concept to market.
What is the current Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of your firm’s main technology or product under development?
Please select the description that best matches the current state of your technology:

TRL 1 — Basic principles observed: Scientific research has begun; basic properties of the technology have been observed and reported
TRL 2 — Technology concept formulated: Application of the technology has been conceived; no experimental proof yet
TRL 3 — Experimental proof of concept: Active research and development has begun; first laboratory studies completed
TRL 4 — Technology validated in laboratory: The technology has been validated in a laboratory environment
TRL 5 — Technology validated in relevant environment: The technology has been validated in an environment relevant to its intended application (e.g. industrial simulation)
TRL 6 — Technology demonstrated in relevant environment: A prototype or pilot system has been demonstrated in a relevant environment
TRL 7 — System prototype demonstration in operational environment: The prototype is close to the planned operational system and has been demonstrated in an operational environment
TRL 8 — System complete and qualified: The technology has been proven to work in its final form and under expected conditions
TRL 9 — Actual system proven in operational environment: The technology is fully mature and has been proven in its final form through successful operation

What is the target TRL your firm aims to reach for this technology within the next [two / three] years? (Select from the same TRL 1–9 scale above)

A note on TRL for Managing Authorities: The TRL scale was originally developed by NASA and adapted by the European Commission for use across all Horizon Europe and ERDF R&D instruments. TRL 1–3 corresponds to basic and applied research; TRL 4–6 to technology development and validation; TRL 7–9 to demonstration and market deployment. Many EU grant schemes specify a minimum entry TRL (e.g. TRL 4 or above) and a target exit TRL, making TRL advancement a natural primary outcome for R&D support evaluations. Self-reported TRL should ideally be validated against objective evidence (e.g. prototype documentation, test reports) where possible.

title: Data
text:
Surveys are one of the most important tools available for collecting primary data in the context of impact evaluations. They make it possible to gather structured information directly from the people and organisations that an intervention is designed to help — whether that means understanding the needs of potential beneficiaries, uncovering barriers to take-up, or shedding light on how and why a programme is producing the results it does.
A key strength of surveys is their efficiency. Rather than collecting information from every single person or organisation in a target population, surveys can be conducted on a carefully selected subset — known as a sample. Provided that sample is representative of the wider population, the findings can be generalised with confidence to all beneficiaries of a given instrument. For Managing Authorities overseeing large-scale programmes with thousands of beneficiaries, this makes surveys a practical and cost-effective way to generate credible evidence without the need for exhaustive data collection.
For EU Managing Authorities in particular, surveys are also a valuable tool for meeting monitoring and evaluation obligations under EU Structural and Investment Fund regulations. They can complement administrative data — such as records held in programme management systems — by capturing information on outcomes and experiences that administrative sources simply do not record.




Surveys can be conducted on paper or in electronic form. While paper-based surveys may be familiar and accessible in some contexts, electronic surveys offer significant advantages that make them the preferred choice in most evaluation settings today.
Digital surveys allow for built-in data validation, such as mandatory fields, range checks, and logical constraints, which help ensure that only valid data is captured from the outset. This greatly reduces the risk of human errors that typically arise during manual data entry or when transferring information from paper forms into a database. Electronic data collection is also faster: responses can be recorded and processed in real time, eliminating the need for transcription. Once collected, digital data can be directly imported into statistical analysis software or monitoring platforms, making analysis and reporting considerably more straightforward.
For Managing Authorities working within tight programme timelines and reporting deadlines, the efficiency gains from digital data collection are particularly valuable.




There are three main methods of electronic data collection, each suited to different contexts and target groups.
Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviewing (CATI) involves interviewers conducting surveys over the phone using a digital questionnaire displayed on their screen. This approach can reach respondents from a wide range of demographic groups and geographic locations relatively quickly, making it well-suited to large-scale data collection efforts. It is also an effective way to monitor how a policy is being implemented and to identify emerging issues in close to real time. For Managing Authorities seeking timely feedback on programme roll-out, CATI can be a practical option.
Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) takes the form of face-to-face interviews conducted with the support of a tablet, laptop, or smartphone loaded with survey software. The main advantage of this method is the quality of the information it yields: the personal interaction between interviewer and respondent tends to produce more nuanced and accurate answers, particularly on complex or sensitive topics. The trade-offs are cost and the potential for interviewer influence — the presence of an interviewer can, in some cases, affect how respondents answer questions. CAPI is best reserved for situations where data quality is paramount and the budget allows for it.
Web surveys are questionnaires sent to respondents via the internet, inviting them to complete the survey at a time and pace that suits them. They are the most cost-effective option and can reach large numbers of people quickly. However, they carry a risk of response bias: individuals without reliable internet access, or those less comfortable with online tools, may be systematically excluded. Respondents with less time may also be less likely to complete the questionnaire. For EU programmes targeting specific business communities or research organisations — groups typically comfortable with online tools — web surveys are often a strong choice, but care should be taken to monitor response rates and the characteristics of those who do and do not respond.
Choosing the right method is not simply a technical decision. It should be guided by who the target respondents are, what resources are available, and how sensitive or complex the questions being asked are.






The timing of a survey has a significant bearing on the quality and completeness of the data collected. At the most basic level, surveys should be scheduled to reach respondents when they are most likely to be available and willing to engage. For surveys targeting firm employees, standard working hours — broadly between 9am and 5pm — are generally the most effective window. Phone or in-person surveys conducted outside working hours are less likely to reach the right contacts and may achieve lower response rates.
The time of year matters just as much. In many European countries, August is a period of reduced business activity due to summer holidays, making it a poor time to conduct surveys with firms or public organisations. Similarly, the end of the financial year is often a particularly busy period for companies, which can make it difficult to secure the attention of senior staff. For Managing Authorities, it is also worth aligning survey timing with key milestones in the programme cycle — for example, conducting a baseline survey before an intervention begins and an endline survey after it has concluded — so that changes in outcomes can be properly attributed to the programme.



Identifying the right respondent is just as important as asking the right questions. The ideal respondent is someone who is well-informed about the behaviour or outcome the evaluation is trying to measure, has a reliable incentive to answer honestly, and can be reached without undue difficulty.
For surveys targeting businesses — a common scenario in EU competitiveness and innovation programmes — this typically means seeking out a senior decision-maker, such as a CEO, CFO, or another member of the executive team. Senior managers are generally the most knowledgeable about strategic decisions, investment choices, and the overall performance of the firm. They also tend to have a more complete view of how the organisation has benefited from an intervention.
It is also important to think carefully about who within an organisation is most directly affected by the programme being evaluated. If an intervention targeted a specific group — such as researchers in an R&D department, or employees who received training — then those individuals may be better placed to answer certain questions than a general manager. The choice of respondent should ultimately be guided by the unit of analysis and the specific outcomes being measured.



Good survey design balances thoroughness with brevity. Completing a survey takes time and effort on the part of the respondent, and overly long or complex questionnaires lead to lower response rates, higher drop-off mid-survey, and less reliable answers. The goal is to collect exactly the information needed — no more, no less — in a way that is as clear and engaging as possible.
Evaluators should focus on digital data collection as the default approach and give careful thought to the types of questions used, the overall length of the questionnaire, and the sequencing of topics. It is also important to decide early on whether the evaluation requires only an endline survey or a baseline survey conducted before the intervention begins as well. Baseline and endline surveys serve different purposes and differ in structure: the baseline captures the situation before the intervention and establishes a point of comparison, while the endline measures what has changed. For Managing Authorities aiming to demonstrate programme impact, having a well-designed baseline is particularly valuable, as it makes it far easier to attribute observed changes to the intervention itself rather than to external factors.



The starting point for questionnaire design should always be existing, validated instruments. Drawing on questions that have already been tested and used in similar evaluations — such as those found in the Community Innovation Survey (CIS) or the World Bank Enterprise Surveys — saves time and improves comparability with other studies. Where possible, Managing Authorities should consult an evidence base of existing survey tools before developing new questions from scratch.
Questions should be clear, specific, and neutral in their wording. Each question should address only one idea at a time — so-called “double-barrelled” questions, which ask about two things simultaneously, make it impossible for respondents to give an accurate answer and should always be avoided. Leading questions, which subtly steer the respondent towards a particular answer, undermine the reliability of the data and should be eliminated during the review process.
Response scales — such as Likert scales or rating systems — should be consistent throughout the questionnaire and clearly labelled so that respondents understand exactly what each option means. Questions should be ordered in a logical flow that feels natural to the respondent, moving from general to specific topics. Sensitive questions, such as those about financial performance or employment decisions, are best placed towards the end of the questionnaire, once some rapport has been established.
Where the survey is to be conducted in multiple languages — a common situation for EU programmes operating across different member states or regions — the questionnaire should be professionally translated and then back-translated into the original language to verify that the meaning has been preserved accurately.
Finally, no questionnaire should go into the field without first being piloted with a small group of respondents who are representative of the target population. A pilot test reveals ambiguous wording, poorly calibrated response options, technical issues in digital forms, and questions that take too long to answer. The questionnaire should be revised based on the results of the pilot before full deployment begins.





For EU Managing Authorities, data protection is not optional — it is a legal obligation. Any survey that collects personal data from individuals or information that could be used to identify specific organisations must comply with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This means that respondents must be clearly informed about how their data will be used, stored, and protected, and must give their consent before participating. Survey responses should be anonymised or pseudonymised wherever possible, and access to identifiable data should be restricted to authorised personnel only.
Beyond legal compliance, ethical data collection also builds trust with respondents. Beneficiaries who feel their information is being handled responsibly are more likely to participate and to answer honestly, which ultimately improves the quality of the evaluation.

Learning through impact evaluation is a continuous process
Every evaluation raises new questions along with the ones it answers, each round building on the last. Review Review a programme’s theory of change, identify risks and learning opportunities. Review lessons from other settings and countries, adapt them, test them in a new context. Identify baseline needs of potential beneficiaries in your region.


Test Test different programme designs and delivery modes to identify what works best. Assess for whom the programme works best. Address take-up challenges, both over and undersubscription. Learn about mechanisms, unintended effects, and crowding out.

Is it relevant for you

title: Why and When
section: Think impact evaluation is not relevant for you?
text:
Think impact evaluation is not relevant for you?
Whether you have sufficient evidence that your programme works, or you are still working out who it reaches and how to design it, there is a case for evaluation. The starting question is whether the programme is working as well as it could be.



You want to learn who to target and how to design it


Too many applicants? Consider introducing randomization in the middle ranks.
Too few applicants? Consider simplifying access and using an encouragement design.




You know it is effective, but is it efficient?


Test how you deliver it. Compare different ways of delivering the programme to the same beneficiaries, testing changes that improve efficiency and satisfaction.




An impact evaluation is not useful only if you already have enough evidence on returns for your target group and region, and there is no interest in learning about different ways of implementing the programme for the same beneficiaries.

M&E versus impact evaluation

title: Why and When
section: What is the difference between monitoring and evaluation and impact evaluation?
text:
What is the difference between monitoring and evaluation and impact evaluation?



Monitoring


Collect data on inputs, outputs, outcomes and participants to:

Improve day-to-day management and decisions
Make descriptive before and after comparisons



Describes what is happening, but not whether it is because of the intervention.




Impact evaluation


Collect data on participants and control groups to:

Assess the difference between participating and not
Establish causality
Support cost-benefit analysis



Determines impact in a way that can only be attributed to the programme, by establishing what would have happened without it.




Allocating public resources

Deadweight: low additionality
Top performers would likely have invested anyway. Public funds substitute for private money they would have spent regardless, generating little truly additional activity per euro.

text:
What exactly is the impact of a programme?
Definition. Impact is what happens after a programme is introduced, minus what would have happened in its absence, the counterfactual.
The dilemma. The counterfactual is a “what if” and is unknown to us.
The solution. Find a way to construct the counterfactual so impact can be measured. This can be done in different ways. The methods below show why randomized controlled trials are considered the gold standard.

title: Why and When
text:
Finding the counterfactual
Strategy. Find a group of firms that on average look like treated firms would have looked in the absence of the programme. This group is the comparison group.



Randomized controlled trials


Create the comparison group up front, by randomly assigning who receives the programme. Randomization is what guarantees the two groups look the same on average.




Ex-post and quasi-experimental designs


Look for a suitable comparison group after the programme has already been rolled out, using natural variation in who received it and who did not.




Selection bias is the risk that the comparison group does not actually look like the treatment group on average. If that assumption is wrong, the impact estimate is biased.


Randomized controlled trials

section: What is a randomized controlled trial?
text:
What is a randomized controlled trial?
Intuition. Randomly assign the programme so one group receives it (the treatment group) and one does not (the control or comparison group). Because the two groups start out the same, the control group’s outcome shows what would have happened to the treatment group without the programme.

Randomly selecting beneficiaries among eligible applicants is fair. When more eligible firms apply than there is budget to fund, a lottery is a transparent way to decide who gets in, treating every eligible applicant the same rather than relying on favouritism or timing.

What “random” means here. Not randomly sampling a sub-population to study, but randomly deciding, among firms that already qualify, who receives the programme and who does not.

text:
What if you cannot randomize?
An RCT only works if randomization is built in from day one, integrated at design stage before the programme launches, not added afterward. When that is not possible, quasi-experimental methods are the alternative.

Quasi-experimental methods always rely on assumptions, some stronger than others. If those assumptions do not hold, the impact estimate is biased. Many of these assumptions are not testable. The credibility of the evaluation depends on the credibility of the assumptions made.


Pre-post (before and after)


Method

Compare programme participants before and after the programme.

Identifying assumption

In the absence of the programme, participants would have had the same measured outcomes as before. That means no other factors or events, for example economic shocks, affect the outcome besides the programme. This is a strong assumption that rarely holds in practice.



For example, sales might rise after a grant simply because the whole regional economy is recovering at the same time, not because of the programme.

Compare programme participants with non-participants.

Identifying assumption

There is no difference between participants and non-participants besides programme participation. The reason for participation must be unrelated to outcomes. Again, this is unlikely to hold in practice.



For example, firms that apply for a grant are often more ambitious or better managed than those that do not, so they might grow faster regardless of the grant.

Difference in differences


Method

Find a group with the same trend and compare differences over time.

Identifying assumption

Any other factors affecting participants over time are the same for non-participants, so both groups would follow the same trajectory in the absence of treatment. This is the parallel trends assumption, and it cannot be tested.



For example, if grant recipients are concentrated in areas hit harder by a regional downturn than the comparison firms, their trends could diverge even without the programme.

The estimate is Diff 1 minus Diff 2: how much more the treatment group changed than the comparison group.



Matching


Method

Participants are matched with non-participants who share the same observable characteristics. Matching tries to mimic an RCT. It can be done in different ways: a participant can be matched with one non-participant, or with a weighted average of all similar non-participants, where closer matches count more.

Identifying assumption

There are no differences between participants and matched non-participants in unobserved characteristics that affect the outcome.



For example, two firms matched on size and sector might still differ in the owner’s ambition or management quality, both of which would likely affect outcomes.

Regression discontinuity design


Method

Compare participants who were just eligible with those who were just ineligible. This does not measure impact for all participants, only for those at the cut-off, which is why the result is called a local average treatment effect. section: Reasons not to measure impact via policy experimentation
text:
Reasons not to measure impact via policy experimentation


01

Not the right tool
The question is excellent but is not about impact, for example satisfaction with services or cost per service. Monitoring and feedback data are easier and do not need a counterfactual.



02

Not yet
The theory of change is not clear, or implementation is unlikely to work because the markets to serve do not exist.



03

Statistically not feasible
Too few units or too little money. Large indirect or spillover effects you cannot measure. Setting too chaotic, for example disaster relief. Treatment assigned at too high a level, for example national policy.



04

Maybe not worth it for learning
The answer is already known from credible existing studies, or there is no generalizable “why” because the programme is one-off with little scale or replication potential.

Risks

title: Why and When
section: I have excess demand and a well designed RCT. What can go wrong?
text:
I have excess demand and a well designed RCT. What can go wrong?


01

Non-compliance and take-up
Not every firm assigned to a programme ends up participating. Comparing everyone as originally assigned (the intention-to-treat effect) stays unbiased, since assignment was random, but it understates the effect on those who actually participated.



02

Attrition
Participants may drop out before outcomes can be measured, or stop responding to follow-up data collection. The risk is that dropout is not random: if struggling firms are the ones most likely to disappear, the firms you do measure make the programme look better than it is.



03

Spillovers and contamination
The comparison group is not always as isolated as it looks. Know-how from a business training programme can spread by word of mouth to non-participating competitors or suppliers, so the comparison group partly benefits too, understating the true effect.

EuroCOMP Lab evaluations

Running example. Romania runs through every page of the site. This is where the full story sits, with the baseline report attached.


Financial support to digitalize: Romania’s program provides non-refundable grants to SMEs for digitalization, aiming to boost productivity in the North-East region, with a focus on key digital performance indicators. Digitalization has the potential to transform industries, particularly SMEs, which in Romania lag behind the EU average in digital performance. Key barriers to digital transformation include lack of financing, awareness, and capacity to capitalize on digital investments. In North-East Romania, digitalization grants are awarded to eligible SMEs under the de minimis aid scheme, with a total allocation ofA C31,000,000 in the first call (A C26,350,000 ERDF andA C4,650,000 from the state budget). Firms can receive grants ranging fromA C15,000 toA C100,000, covering 90% of eligible project costs. The World Bank studies the impact of digitalization on SME performance. The hypothesis is that financial support will boost productivity by enabling the acquisition of knowledge, services, and soft/hardware. As part of the study, the World Bank conducted a pre-assessment using DESI indicators, as defined by the Regional Development Agency (RDA): The most common technology was “20+ percent of employees using connected mobile devices” (681 businesses, 66% of the sample), followed by “Internet connection of at least 30 Megabits per second” (620 businesses, 60%) and “50+ percent of employees with Internet access” (604 businesses, 58%).


Financial support to innovate: Spain’s matching grant program awards up toA C250k per firm to boost R&D investment in small and medium companies, primarily in agriculture and ecological transition.  To address market failures that keep regional R&D investment at suboptimal levels, the La Junta de Extremadura, the Regional Government of Extremadura (JUNTA) and Foundation for the Development of Science and Technology and the Extremadura Science and Technology Park Foundation (FUNDECYT-PCTEx) have developed a matching grant program funded by the EU, offering large R&D grants to small and medium firms in Extremadura. Each cycle plans to awardA C3.5 million in grants (up to C250k per company), financing 35% to 80% of proposed R&D investments. Applicants are primarily small and medium companies, mainly in the agricultural or ecological transition sectors, with most grants supporting industrial research and experimental development. The World Bank is collaborating with JUNTA to offer technical support aimed at generating valuable insights from this investment. In this process, the evaluation team, working with regional authorities, has revised operational manuals to enhance the institutional framework by incorporating international best practices in the design, implementation, and evaluation of this public instrument.


Add-Ons to make financial support more impactful: In Czechia, the World Bank evaluates whether enhancing entrepreneurial skills improves the effectiveness of a voucher scheme supporting business development, innovation, and digital transformation in regions affected by the coal industry’s decline.  Several Czech regions are focused on economic diversification, prioritizing private sector growth, but entrepreneurial activity remains low. A new program, approved by the European Commission in September 2022, targets regions affected by the decline of the coal mining industry. It emphasizes business R&D, post-mining area regeneration, skills development, clean energy, and the circular economy, with a total allocation ofA C1.641 billion. A key component of the Just Transition Programme (JTP) is the voucher scheme for entrepreneurs in Czech coal regions, offering different types of financial support. These vouchers are available in the Moravian-Silesian, Ustí, and Karlovy Vary regions, with a focus on diversifying local economies reliant on carbon intensive industries. The impact evaluation includes complementary activities to strengthen the JTP outcomes. One such initiative is the ‘Smart Start’ project, launched with World Bank’s support since 2022. In the Ustí and Karlovy Vary regions, this program focuses on innovation vouchers, incorporating a ‘networking’ approach, where firms receive expert advisory support and are encouraged to share knowledge and network to enhance innovation. In the Moravian-Silesian region, the program emphasizes mindset training for innovation, offering ‘smart training’ that promotes a scientific approach to decision-making under uncertainty. This training, aimed at firms selected for entrepreneurial vouchers (and others), teaches participants to make informed decisions in uncertain environments, covering topics such as understanding innovation, risk vs. uncertainty, hypothesis testing, and A/B testing, culminating in participant presentations.


AMatchmaking support to connect: The Scinergy pilot in Croatia connects businesses and scientists to foster collaborations, support innovation, and drive R&D through matchmaking events and ongoing guidance.  A World Bank survey revealed that 47% of companies lacked information about relevant scientists, highlighting the need for improved collaboration to drive innovation and technology transfer. To strengthen science-business collaboration, Croatia is piloting a business-science matchmaking support program. For this purpose, the World Bank, in partnership with the Innovation Center Nikola Tesla and the Ministry of Science, Education, and Youth, designed the “Scinergy” pilot to facilitate science-business collaboration. Scinergy aims to help connect businesses and scientists based on their needs and expertise, supporting product development, joint funding applications, and public-private partnerships. Participating firms are offered targeted connections with scientists across fields like AI, energy, and biotechnology, and are offered legal and communication support. Matched researchers and businesses first participated in a two-day matchmaking event in February 2024. The first day involved “speed-dating” sessions between firms and scientists, while the second day featured workshops for pairs interested in collaboration. These sessions encouraged ideation, with exercises like explaining potential solutions in simple terms and visualizing them through drawings. In March and April 2024, these pairs explored concrete R&D ideas, leading to detailed discussions and joint project planning. Pilot monitoring revealed that newly established interactions between firms and scientists continued in this period, with discussions on collaboration details, intellectual property, legal frameworks, and project financing. Firms attended specialized lectures on these topics, which deepened their understanding and aimed to facilitate cooperation. Qualitative insights and feedback surveys from participants indicated that the main collaboration goals were joint R&D projects, technological consultations, and prototype development. Companies reported challenges such as financial constraints, legal issues, and aligning goals.

text:
Step 1: Define a Theory of Change (ToC) for your IE

What is a Theory of Change?
A Theory of Change is a causal chain between inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, and goals of an instrument or policy. It provides a clear understanding of the mechanisms through which policy makers intend an instrument or policy to generate desired outcomes or long-term goals.


Components of a Theory of Change
The ToC follows a linear causal chain, with assumptions sitting between each step:

Inputs
Resources, efforts, and actions invested in a policy — financial resources, personnel, equipment, training programs, etc.


Activities
Actions and tasks undertaken using the inputs to deliver the intended outputs. The concrete work of the policy or instrument — e.g., running grant calls, delivering training, disbursing subsidies, providing advisory services.


Outputs
Direct and immediate results of the activities conducted within a policy. Tangible and observable products or deliverables that demonstrate the completion of specific tasks.


Short-Term Outcomes
Immediate changes that occur as a direct result of the outputs. Often related to changes in knowledge, attitudes, skills, and behaviors among the target population. They play a crucial role in achieving the larger objectives.


Medium-Term Outcomes
Intermediate changes that occur due to sustained efforts and progress from short-term outcomes. Indicate progress toward the overall goal and often involve shifts in social norms, policies, or organizational practices.


Goals
The policy’s broad, long-term aspirations or objectives. Describe the ultimate impact or change that the policy aims to achieve. Goals are usually overarching and may require significant time and effort to accomplish.


Assumptions
Assumptions are the conditions that must hold for each link in the causal chain to lead to the next. They sit between every step and represent the risks to the logic. An impact evaluation exists to test these assumptions; making them explicit tells you what to measure and where the logic is most likely to break.

Running example. TO BE ADDED BY MIKE: Theory of Change from the North-East





Why Invest Time in Developing a ToC?
1. It sharpens the design of your evaluation - Generates clear research questions and defines which outcomes to measure and what data to collect - Can be built participatorily by starting from the final outcomes and working backwards - Prompts a credibility check: is there evidence to support each step in the causal chain?
2. It produces richer, more transferable policy lessons - Measuring the right intermediate outcomes reveals how and why an instrument works, not just whether it works - Opening this “black box” turns results into actionable insight rather than a single verdict - The resulting knowledge generalises better to other contexts, settings, and instruments


Defining Evaluation Questions
Defining clear evaluation questions is the starting point of any rigorous impact evaluation. A well-formulated evaluation question specifies what the intervention is, who it targets, what outcome is expected to change, and over what time horizon. Questions should be grounded in the Theory of Change — each one should correspond to a link in the causal chain that the evaluation seeks to test. In practice, it helps to distinguish between the primary evaluation question, which typically concerns the overall effect of the intervention on a key outcome, and secondary questions, which probe mechanisms, heterogeneous effects across subgroups, or the role of specific assumptions. Evaluation questions should also be realistic: they must be answerable with the data and methods available, and scoped to what the evaluation can credibly attribute to the intervention rather than to external factors.

Step 2: Build Relevant Indicators

From ToC to Indicators
A ToC plays a vital role as a foundation for developing relevant indicators to assess the impacts of a policy. The elements of a ToC reflect constructs that need further definition to be measurable. Indicators should be defined for each pillar of the ToC (inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, goals, and assumptions) to enable the measurement and verification of change.


Well-Defined Indicators (SMART)







Criterion
Description




Specific
To measure the information required as closely as possible


Measurable
To ensure that the information can be readily obtained (usually in numerical form)


Attributable
To ensure that each measure is linked to the project’s efforts


Realistic
To ensure that the data can be obtained in a timely fashion, with reasonable frequency, and at a reasonable cost


Targeted
To the objective population




Running example. TO BE ADDED BY MIKE: Indicators from the North-East



From Indicators to Data
Indicators rarely need to be built from scratch. Where possible, practitioners should draw on existing, well-tested measures from similar studies, evidence gap maps, and validated frameworks such as the CIS or WB Enterprise Surveys. Once indicators are defined, each one requires a concrete data source to back it up. Step 3 addresses this by answering, for every indicator, what needs to be collected, what type of data is appropriate (primary or secondary), how it should be gathered, from whom, and at what point in time. Crucially, these decisions must be made early — before randomization begins — to ensure the evaluation is properly set up to measure what it intends to.

title: Theory of Change and Measurement
text:
Step 3: Collect Appropriate Data

First-Order Decisions
Before any data collection begins, five fundamental questions need to be answered:

What do you need to measure?
What type of data is needed to measure this?
How should it be collected?
Who should you collect it from?
When should you collect it?


Critically, these decisions must be made before the project starts — not after — as choices made too late can compromise the entire evaluation.




What Do You Need to Measure?
The main purpose of data collection is to test the assumptions embedded in the Theory of Change — which means gathering information at every step where the causal logic could break down. Beyond outcomes, it is important to capture covariates: background characteristics such as gender, location, or firm size that may explain why an intervention works differently for different groups. Decisions about how to account for these differences, through stratification for instance, should be made upfront. Compliance also needs to be tracked — understanding who actually took up the intervention, and why, is essential for interpreting results. Finally, the timing of data collection must reflect the different purposes it serves: baseline data, take-up information, and both intermediate and final outcome measures all require separate planning before the intervention begins.



What Type of Data Is Needed?
There are two broad types of data available to evaluators. Primary data is information collected directly from target respondents — such as individuals, research organizations, or firms — either by the organization itself or through contracted intermediaries. Secondary data, by contrast, draws on existing sources, particularly administrative records and data gathered by other organizations or government agencies. Both have distinct strengths and limitations, and the right choice depends on the specific needs of the evaluation.

How Should Data Be Collected?
When collecting primary data, the method should be chosen based on what works best for the respondents and the context — whether that is an in-person survey, a phone interview, or an online questionnaire. Digital collection tools are preferable where possible, as they reduce errors and speed up processing. The instrument should always be piloted before full deployment, and quality controls should be built in throughout the process.
For secondary and administrative data, the key is to identify the data owner as early as possible, since access negotiations and data-sharing agreements can take considerable time. Before committing to a source, its quality should be carefully assessed — checking for completeness, consistency, and clear variable definitions. GDPR compliance must also be confirmed before any data is transferred.
Regardless of the data type, collection choices should be matched to the indicators and the Theory of Change. It is also worth noting that primary and secondary data can be combined — for example, using administrative records as a baseline and primary survey data for follow-up. Before investing in new data collection, teams should thoroughly assess what data already exists and whether it can serve the evaluation’s needs at lower cost.



Who Should You Collect Data From?
For primary data, the goal is to reach respondents who are knowledgeable about the outcome of interest and have little reason to misreport. The choice of respondent should also match the unit of analysis: for firm-level interventions, for instance, a senior decision-maker such as a C-suite executive is typically the most appropriate source. It is also worth thinking carefully about who within an organisation actually benefits from the intervention — the firm as a whole, or a specific group such as R&D staff — as this shapes who should be surveyed.
For secondary and administrative data, the starting point is identifying which organisation or agency holds the most relevant records — whether that is a business registry, tax authority, customs office, or patent office. Where multiple sources are available, linking them through a common identifier such as a VAT number can produce a much richer picture.
In both cases, the unit of data collection should align with the unit of randomization, and data should be collected from the same respondent or source at both baseline and endline to ensure results are comparable over time.



When Should You Collect Data?
For primary data, baseline information must be collected before randomization and before the intervention begins. The timing of the endline should reflect when effects can realistically be expected to have materialised — collecting too early risks missing impacts that take time to emerge. Depending on the intervention, intermediate rounds of data collection may also be needed to track progress along the Theory of Change.
For secondary and administrative data, pre-intervention records should be requested as early as possible to establish baseline trends. The frequency and timing of data transfers should be agreed with the data owner in advance, and reporting lags must be factored in — administrative data is often published with a delay. It is also important to be aware of the release calendar of administrative sources, as availability may be annual, quarterly, or irregular, which directly affects when meaningful analysis can be conducted.
Across both data types, survey fatigue should be avoided by spacing out collection rounds and keeping each one as concise as possible. Teams should also be mindful of seasonality, steering clear of periods that could distort results such as fiscal year-ends or holiday periods. Finally, the timing of every data collection round should be documented to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

In a world of scarce resources, you need evidence on what is actually worth funding
The EU is one of the world’s largest investors in innovation, yet significant regional disparities in innovation outcomes are limiting its overall competitiveness. To remain on par with global counterparts, every euro invested needs to yield greater returns and have a more substantial impact on growth.
The processes behind these investments often lack mechanisms for continuous learning, even as policy needs to keep adapting to evolving circumstances. This calls for identifying challenges, testing solutions, and refining approaches.

This is what we call science-based adaptive delivery: testing, learning, and adjusting as you go.

title: Join a growing community of practice for impact evaluation in Europe
section: Testing and learning only works if you know what to look for
text:
Testing and learning only works if you know what to look for
When evaluating projects, we often only assess outputs, because they are the easiest thing to count. Impact evaluation is what lets you move from measuring outputs to proving outcomes.


Outputs
What a program delivers: grants disbursed, firms enrolled, trainings run.


Outcomes
What changes because of it: growth, jobs, innovation, resilience.


To understand in advance why each step should lead to the next, you need to map out, before implementation, how a program’s activities are expected to change the problem you are addressing. That causal logic, the how and why behind each step, explains a program’s reason for existing, and tells you what to measure to test whether the expected change is actually happening.


Inputs


Activities


Outputs


Outcomes


This chain is the foundation of a Theory of Change, and having thought it through helps in designing a strong impact evaluation. There is more on this in Why and When.

What is an impact evaluation

title: Join a growing community of practice for impact evaluation in Europe
section: But what is impact evaluation exactly?
text:
But what is impact evaluation exactly?

It allows us to answer the questions: what impact did this intervention have on regional development, and how did different approaches change the outcome? For whom did it work best, and under which conditions?

To answer that, an impact evaluation isolates a program’s actual effect from everything else going on (economic trends, other policies, or the kinds of firms likely to apply in the first place), rather than just describing what happened. It compares what actually happened after introducing a program to what would have happened without it, the counterfactual.


Not the same as M&E
M&E tracks whether a program is implemented as planned. Impact evaluation tests whether it caused a real difference, compared to what would have happened without it.


Built in from day one
The comparison group, sample size, and data collection all depend on decisions made before a program launches, not added on afterward.


Each one builds on the last
Each evaluation answers some questions and raises new ones, helping you understand your regional market and design more impactful programs next time.
